topic: Mastering Abstract Vector Spaces: From Arrows to Anything
target_audience: Undergraduate STEM students with a basic knowledge of 2D/3D vectors

sections.title: Introduction: The Identity Crisis of a Vector
lecture_lines: You might think a vector is just an arrow.
But in abstract algebra, vectors can be anything.
It's about how they behave, not their look.
animations: Show a standard 2D arrow vector in blue (#58C4DD).
Morph the arrow into a sine wave function in yellow (#EEEE00).
Morph the wave into a 2x2 grid of numbers (matrix) in green (#77FF77).

sections.title: Prerequisites: The DNA of Vector Operations
lecture_lines: Two operations define these spaces: addition and scaling.
In 2D, we add arrows using the parallelogram rule.
Scaling an arrow simply stretches or shrinks its length.
animations: Vector addition: Two arrows (u and v) in blue (#58C4DD) forming a parallelogram with sum u+v in red (#FF0000).
Scalar multiplication: A vector arrow in blue (#58C4DD) stretching to double its length in light green (#C9FFC9).
Highlight the result label "R² Baseline" in white (#FFFFFF).

sections.title: The 10 Axioms: The Rules of the Game
lecture_lines: To be a vector space, ten rules must hold.
Closure means staying within the set after operations.
Addition must be commutative, associative, and have an identity.
Every vector needs an inverse to return to zero.
Scalar multiplication must distribute and respect identity rules.
animations: Show the word "Closure" in yellow (#EEEE00) with a circle containing symbols for 'u' and 'v'.
Addition properties: List Commutative and Associative in light blue (#ADD8E6).
Zero Vector and Inverse: Show '0' and '-v' popping up in purple (#B19CD9).
Scalar properties: Show Distributive laws with symbols in orange (#FFA500).
The "Vetting Machine" graphic: An object passes through a scanner and a green "OFFICIAL" stamp appears in green (#77FF77).

sections.title: Concrete Abstraction: The Space of Polynomials
lecture_lines: Take polynomials: they don't look like arrows at all.
Adding two polynomials always results in another polynomial.
Scaling a polynomial also keeps it in the set.
They follow every axiom, just like our geometric arrows.
Thus, polynomials are true vectors in their own space.
animations: Plot f(x) = x² in blue (#58C4DD) on a simple set of axes.
Plot g(x) = 2x in yellow (#EEEE00) on the same axes.
Animate the point-wise addition of f(x) and g(x) to form h(x) = x² + 2x in red (#FF0000).
Highlight the resulting curve and label it "A Vector in P₂" in white (#FFFFFF).
Flash the scaling of h(x) by 0.5, showing the curve flattening, still a polynomial.

sections.title: Geometric Intuition: Visualizing the Abstract
lecture_lines: Abstract spaces can still be visualized with coordinates.
We use a basis to define every vector's position.
For polynomials, axes represent powers like 1, x, and x².
A polynomial is then a point in this coordinate system.
This geometric view turns abstract functions into navigable spaces.
animations: Display three axes labeled '1', 'x', and 'x²' in gray (#808080).
Plot a point at coordinates (1, 2, 3) in white (#FFFFFF).
Draw a line from the origin to the point, labeled "1 + 2x + 3x²" in yellow (#EEEE00).
Fade in the word "Basis" next to the axes labels in cyan (#00FFFF).
Scale the whole system to represent a 3D "Polynomial Space".

sections.title: Summary & Application: Why it Matters
lecture_lines: Vector spaces are defined by rules, not specific objects.
This framework powers quantum mechanics and signal processing.
Mastering abstraction lets you solve diverse problems with one tool.
animations: Montage: Split screen showing a digital image grid and a wave-function.
Overlay the text "Shared Rules" in gold (#FFD700) across both.
Fade out elements to leave the text "Vector Spaces = Universal Framework" in white (#FFFFFF).
